description: Question: how do you grow a perfect crystal of one semiconductor on a wafer of another, and why is the photodetector in every fibre-optic receiver made of exactly In0.53Ga0.47As? Data: Alexandria's PBE calculations (keyless OPTIMADE) of the zincblende III-V binaries, Si and Ge, and of ordered (In,Ga)As and (Al,Ga)As cells; measured lattice constants of GaAs, InAs, AlAs and InP from the Crystallography Open Database. Steps: the cubic lattice constant from each cell's volume (a = (8V/atoms)^(1/3)); each alloy against the straight line between its end points (Vegard's law) and a least-squares bowing parameter for its lattice constant and band gap; the composition x* where In(x)Ga(1−x)As has InP's lattice constant, from PBE and from measured values; PBE's error against the measured cells. Aha: an alloy's lattice constant is linear in its composition (the ordered alloys sit on Vegard's line to a few hundredths of a percent) while its band gap bends, so composition is a dial: pick x to match the substrate, then the gap follows; on the gap-against-lattice-constant map every epitaxial stack is a vertical line, GaAs and AlAs share one (strain-free AlGaAs lasers and transistors), and InP's crosses (In,Ga)As at x ≈ 0.53. Caveats: PBE lattice constants are 1–2% too large and not uniformly so, which moves the matched x (0.47 with PBE, 0.53 with the measured cells) and even flips the sign of the tiny AlAs-on-GaAs mismatch (−0.21% PBE, +0.13% measured); PBE gaps are far too small (InAs and the In-rich alloys have none), so the gap axis is qualitative; ordered cells are not random alloys and fold the indirect valleys onto Γ; strain, critical thickness and thermal-expansion mismatch are not computed. Next: drill into one alloy's cells (click), expand to (Ga,In)P on GaAs, GaN on sapphire or SiGe on Si, and to critical thickness.
name: Vegard's law and lattice matching for epitaxy
